events.text: You have the great map brought into the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the one with the four empires drawn small at the edges, the way a child draws the sea. Grand Secretaries who have not agreed since the last reign agree now that you are mad. Your hand is on the Gray Wolf steppe. "How large is it, really?" you ask, and nobody in the hall has ever been there.

choices.text: Send for the men who have been there

effects.log: They find you an old horse trader and a monk with no toes. You listen for three days. The map is wrong in eleven places, and now you know which ones.

choices.text: "Then we shall find out"

effects.log: The Secretaries bow lower than the words deserved. By evening there is a poem going round the ministries about emperors who wanted the sea.

events.text: The Minister of Revenue comes to you alone, with one ledger, and it is a brave thing to do. He has counted the grain for all four frontiers. It can be done, he says. It will take everything your reign has put by, and the reign after it. He would like you to hear that from him and not from a famine. The ink on his thumb has not washed off in forty years.

choices.text: Make him Quartermaster of All Fronts

effects.log: He looks as if you have sentenced him. He has the first convoys moving in a month, and they arrive.

choices.text: Thank him and march anyway

effects.log: He bows, and goes home, and does not sleep. Nor do the granaries. You will hear of that ledger again.

events.text: The old heads of your line are painted along the ancestral hall, and not one of them ever held more than a good valley and a grudge. You stand in front of them with the muster rolls. A dynasty is a long patience, your grandmother used to say. She meant marriage. Tonight you tell the assembled house what else it might mean, and a cousin laughs before he sees your face.

choices.text: Put the cousin in charge of the first column

effects.log: He stops laughing. He also turns out to be very good at it. Your house marches behind its own name.

choices.text: Let the whole house argue it out

effects.log: It takes a month. They come round in the end, and half of them are coming round for reasons of their own.

events.text: Your house has daughters and sons married into forty families between here and the border, and every one of those weddings cost you more than you could afford. Now you write forty letters. They are very polite. They mention the wedding gifts. By the end of the spring there are carts on the roads that nobody ever had to order, and a great many in-laws asking what, precisely, this is about.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: all of it

effects.log: Some of them go pale. Most of them start sums in the margin. A share of an empire is a very good dowry.

choices.text: Tell each of them something different

effects.log: It works at once, as it always does, and it will keep working until two of them sit down to dinner.

events.text: Nobody has ever marched on an empire from a clan compound. You know this because Elder Baek says so at length, from the far end of the long table, and he is not wrong. He has run your stores for fifty years. When he has finished, he asks how many horses. You tell him. He closes his eyes and says it can be done in the spring, and that he would like it written down that he said no.

choices.text: Write it down, and give him the horses

effects.log: You have it written, and framed. Elder Baek hangs it in the stores, and the clan rides in the spring.

choices.text: Tell him the clan head does not need his no

effects.log: He bows. The horses come, in the end, somewhat later than he said they would.

events.text: Your clan name has been a good one to be feared in three counties. You have the crest sewn onto a banner the size of a threshing floor, and it takes eight people and a good wind to raise it. Children come from four villages to look. In the empire they are about to invade, you think, nobody has ever heard of you. It is a strange thing to look forward to.

choices.text: Have it carried at the very front

effects.log: It is a very large target, and everyone who sees it asks whose it is. That is rather the point.

choices.text: Keep it rolled up until you have won something

effects.log: The riders notice. They do not say anything, and they do not sing much either.

events.text: A sect is for walking in clouds and arguing about breath. You have stood up in the Hall of Forms and told four hundred disciples it is also for this. The Discipline Hall has found three precepts against it, and the Scripture Hall has found one for it, in a commentary nobody has opened since it was written. Somebody at the back has begun, slowly, to tie up a sleeve.

choices.text: "You may stay. I will think no less of you."

effects.log: A third of them stay, and you think no less of them. The rest will follow you off the edge of the map.

choices.text: Order it, as head of the sect

effects.log: They obey at once and completely, and you will not hear what they really think for several years.

events.text: Your disciples have never been in a war of more than two hundred on a side. A sect fights in the morning and is home for the evening lesson. So you take them to see a real supply train at the salt road, ten thousand carts and not one master among them, and watch their faces. "That," you say, "is what kills you." The youngest asks whether there is a form for it. You find that there is going to have to be.

choices.text: Write the Ledger Form yourself

effects.log: The elders think it is a joke for a whole season. Then it is the most copied manual on the mountain.

choices.text: Hire people who already know

effects.log: Mercenary quartermasters come up the mountain, spitting. Your disciples look at them as if they were weather.

events.text: The Cult has been the end of the world in other people's stories for six hundred years, and it has mostly stayed in its mountains. Now you tell the Elders it will come down. There is a long silence in the hall of black pillars. Then the oldest of them begins to laugh, without a sound, and in a little while they are all doing it. It is not a comfortable thing to stand in front of.

choices.text: Laugh with them

effects.log: The drums start before you have finished. The Hundred Thousand Mountains empty like a kicked hive.

choices.text: Wait until it stops, and read out the marching order

effects.log: It stops rather quickly. They had not known you would do that. They are still not sure they like it.

events.text: Every Cult army there has ever been was beaten by the same thing: the second winter, when there was nothing left to burn and no one left to rob. Grand Elder Hyeon reminds you of this with a certain relish. He was there for the last one, as a boy. He would like to know whether you mean to rule what you take, or whether this is only going to be another very famous summer.

choices.text: "Rule it. Bring the tax clerks."

effects.log: There has never been a Cult tax clerk. By spring there are nine hundred of them, and they are terrible, and everyone pays.

choices.text: "Let them be afraid first, and we will see."

effects.log: He nods. He has heard that before, too. It is an excellent summer.

events.text: The Murim Alliance has never in its history agreed on where to hold a dinner. You put the four empires on the table at the Spring Assembly, and it takes nineteen days. Wudang will go if Shaolin does not lead. Shaolin will go if it may be called something else. The Namgung will go if someone pays them. On the last night you get a paper with every seal on it, and no two seals mean the same thing.

choices.text: Take the paper, and move before they read it

effects.log: You are two provinces away by the time the first letter of clarification arrives. You do not open it.

choices.text: Stay until every clause is settled

effects.log: You lose a season. What you have at the end of it is a real alliance and a very tired one.

events.text: They elected you to keep the demonic sects out of the Central Plains, and you are about to take the Alliance's banners farther from the Central Plains than they have ever been. Old Master Gwak, who voted for you, comes to ask you one thing, on the steps, with nobody listening. He wants to know who is going to hold the door while everyone is away.

choices.text: Leave him the door, and the best of your people

effects.log: It costs you a whole wing of your host. He nods, and goes back up the steps, and the door holds.

choices.text: "The door will not matter, when there is only one house."

effects.log: He looks at you for a long time and says that he is too old to learn a new way of being frightened.

events.text: A General does not march on an empire. A General is sent. So you go up to the capital in plain dress and lay your plan before the throne, and {auh_home} takes it the way anyone takes a sword held out by the blade: very politely, looking at your other hand. The warrant comes in a month. It is generous. It has also been written so that everything that goes wrong is yours.

choices.text: Sign for it, gladly

effects.log: You sign. Your officers read the warrant, and then they look at you with some respect. They know what it means.

choices.text: Have your own clerks rewrite three lines

effects.log: They do, and it holds, and from now on there is a very attentive person at court who reads every word you send.

events.text: The soldiers have a song about you already. It is not a very good one, and it is about what the throne owes them. You hear it at the Liaodong camp, from a cook, who stops when he sees you. Forty years of frontier armies have marched in order to come home. You stand on a wagon and tell them where you mean to take them instead, and that nobody is coming home until there are no more frontiers.

choices.text: Sing the song back at them, badly

effects.log: It takes a moment. Then the whole camp is roaring, and the cook has made you a very bad supper in your honour.

choices.text: Double the pay, from your own purse

effects.log: They cheer the silver. A soldier who follows the silver will count it, so you will have to go on finding more.

events.text: Past the last watchtower there are no more roads. Grass goes on to the edge of the sky, and {auh_foe} has burned a strip of it wide enough to take three days to cross. Your scouts bring you a dead campfire and a single arrow stuck into the ground beside it, pointing the way you were going. It is, your oldest sergeant says, an invitation.

choices.text: Decline it: swing wide to the east, by the river

ok.log: It costs nine days. You come round behind where they were waiting and take the wells without a fight.

fail.log: The river is further than the map said. You arrive thirsty, and {auh_foe} has moved the wells.

choices.text: Accept it, at a walk, in good order

effects.log: You go straight up the arrow. It is very bad for the horses and rather good for the army's opinion of itself.

events.text: A steppe army does not have a city for you to take. It has a horizon. {auh_Host} has spent a month marching towards a smudge of smoke that is exactly as far away as when you started. In the third week the riders come in and tell you it has moved again. The felt cities pack up in an hour. You have been chasing washing, says a quartermaster, and nobody laughs.

choices.text: Stop chasing. Sit on the winter pasture and wait

ok.log: They have to come to the grass. It takes the whole summer, and they come.

fail.log: The grass was never the only pasture. They winter somewhere else, and you winter here.

choices.text: Split the host, and drive them from two sides

effects.log: It nearly works, and it wears out a great many horses. It does not do the horses of the Khaganate any good either.

events.text: The clans of {auh_region} send you a girl of about twelve on a very good horse, with a message. Her grandmother, the clan's elder, has counted your wagons. They would like to know which of you is going to get to be the one who owes the other a debt. She says it in your language without an accent, and is plainly not in the least afraid. She has brought her own lunch.

choices.text: Answer in her tongue, as well as you can

ok.log: She corrects you twice. Then she takes your answer home, and one clan of {auh_region} is suddenly very slow to arrive.

fail.log: What you said means something quite different up here. She rides away laughing, and it gets round.

choices.text: Give her a good knife, and send her back

effects.log: She looks at the blade with a professional eye. It is a fair answer, and now they know you can make one.

events.text: Winter comes down on the Felt Road a month before anyone told you it would. It is a white silence with a wind in it. The horses know first. You have been told by men who have been here that an army out on the open grass can lose a third of itself and never see an enemy, and you can see now that they were being polite. There are some low hills to the south, and they are in exactly the wrong direction.

choices.text: Turn for the hills and lose the season

effects.log: You lose the season and very few people. {auh_foe} hears that you can be sensible, and is less pleased than you might think.

choices.text: Push on through, and catch them in their winter camp

ok.log: You come out of the snow on a morning when no one on earth was expecting anybody. The songs start there.

fail.log: You lose what they said you would lose. The ones who get through do not talk about it.

events.text: The rains begin the week your host reaches {auh_region}. The Nine Rivers do not rise here, exactly. They simply become the country. Every road you were sold is now a rumour with frogs in it. A village headman in a very wide hat wades out to meet you, sets a basket of rice down on nothing, and asks with interest what you had expected, coming in the monsoon.

choices.text: Hire his boats, every one on this water

ok.log: He names a price. You pay it without a word, and {auh_host} goes on, wet and on time, in a thousand rice boats.

fail.log: He names a price. Then he names it to {auh_foe} too, and they pay more.

choices.text: Camp on the terraces, and wait out the rains

effects.log: It takes two months, and half the army learns to fish. The fever is the only enemy you see, and it costs you.

events.text: The first thing your physicians say when you cross into {auh_region} is that you must not drink anything. The second is that you must not eat anything, or brush against the pale vines, or sleep on the ground. Every river here has a physician of its own, and they have all had a thousand years to think about armies. Three of your sergeants have already gone an interesting colour.

choices.text: Send to the temple herb-wives, with gifts

ok.log: They look over your camp as if it were a bad student. They teach you what to chew. The colour goes away.

fail.log: They take your gifts with great courtesy. What they send back works, up to a point, and they know which point.

choices.text: Boil all of it and march fast

effects.log: The army hates it, and most of the army lives. You reach the Fords thin, angry and alive.

events.text: You have read about the elephants. You have been told about the elephants. Your veterans have a joke about the elephants. Now there are forty of them standing across the Long Ford in painted armour, in no hurry at all, and {auh_foe} sits on the largest one with a parasol, eating something. Behind you the horses have started to make a noise you have never heard horses make.

choices.text: Fire and drums at dusk, on their flank

ok.log: They turn. Forty elephants who have changed their minds are the worst thing that can happen to the army behind them.

fail.log: They do not turn. An elephant is not as stupid as a general hopes. It is a long way back to the bank.

choices.text: Go round. It is only a river

effects.log: It is nine rivers. You go round all of them, and the parasol goes round with you, always just in sight.

events.text: The Nine Rivers are older than your empire. A monk at the first temple you take points this out, kindly, while your soldiers are looking at the gold on the roof. He has seen four invasions from this courtyard, or his teachers have, and each of them is in the carvings. He would be glad to show you where they intend to carve yours. It is a nice spot, near the door, with room for a small elephant.

choices.text: Order the gold left on that roof

effects.log: The soldiers grumble. The monk nods very slightly. Word goes down all Nine Rivers faster than a horse, and some gates stay open.

choices.text: Ask to see the carvings of the other four

effects.log: He shows you. You learn a great deal about where they went wrong, and something about what happened to them afterwards.

events.text: There is no way to march to {auh_region}. Your generals have spent their lives learning to march, and they stand on the shingle at the Shandong headland looking at the water as if it had been rude to them. You need nine hundred ships. You have thirty, some fishing boats, and an ancient, delighted person from the coast who says the tide table is all wrong and has a better one.

choices.text: Believe them: sail on their tide

ok.log: You cross in a fog nobody else thought would lift, and it lifts. {auh_foe} is still looking the other way.

fail.log: The tide table was right for a harbour that silted up two hundred years ago. You lose ships, and some time.

choices.text: Build for a year, and do it properly

effects.log: It costs a forest and a season. You have a real fleet at the end of it, and you have also given them a year.

events.text: The harbour castles of {auh_region} are not very big. They are cut into the rock, with one water gate each, and each is held by a lord who has fought a duel to get it and would be ashamed to die in bed. {auh_foe} sends you a note, on beautiful paper, in a fine hand. It suggests that there is really no need for all these soldiers. You might settle the whole of the coast between the two of you, tomorrow, on the sand.

choices.text: Go down to the sand

ok.log: It takes one exchange and a long time getting to it. Next morning {auh_foe}'s captains come down the rock with the keys, and bow to you, and they mean it.

fail.log: They could have killed you. They step back and bow, which is worse. Your soldiers saw all of it, and they have started to look at the sea.

choices.text: Write back: an army is not a duel

effects.log: They reply that this is exactly what is wrong with you. Then it is ladders at the water gates, the hard way, one rock at a time.

events.text: Your ships are met at sea by a small boat with a very old woman in it, smoking a pipe. She is the pilot for these waters, she says, and has been since before the castle at Morning Gate was built. No one has ever got through the reefs without a pilot, and she charges by the ship. She glances over your fleet, and starts to count on her fingers, and seems to be enjoying herself very much.

choices.text: Pay what she asks

effects.log: It is outrageous. She takes you through, ship by ship, singing, in water that is mostly teeth.

choices.text: Learn the channels from the fishermen instead

ok.log: It takes a month of mending nets with people who smell of squid. You get through the reefs for nothing.

fail.log: You learn quite a lot, and you learn the last of it from the reef itself.

events.text: The Isles have one rule of war, it turns out, and they think it obvious. A lord beaten fairly goes over to whoever beat him and fights for them from then on with an untroubled mind. Three of them come to your tent that way in a single week. They are very good, and they sit at your fire discussing your mistakes. Your own officers have stopped eating in the same place.

choices.text: Give them commands of their own

effects.log: Your officers are appalled. The three of them take the next castle in an afternoon, and they send you a poem about it.

choices.text: Keep them close, and watch them

effects.log: It is what anyone would do. They find it a little disappointing, and they say so, in verse.

events.text: The road to {auh_region} climbs for eleven days, and on the twelfth your soldiers begin to lie down. It is not an illness, the guides say. It is only that there is not so much air here as they are used to. A woman with a yak has been walking past your column for an hour with a load twice what your men are carrying. She looks back once or twice, with what might be concern.

choices.text: Stop and let them get used to it, ten days

ok.log: It costs ten days. {auh_foe} had counted on you doing it the other way, and the passes are not yet held.

fail.log: You stop for ten days. It turns out that {auh_foe} had counted on that too, and has spent them on the walls.

choices.text: Hire her, and every yak on this side of the pass

effects.log: She looks at your silver for some time. Your stores go up on the backs of beasts that do not know this is difficult.

events.text: The caravan masters of the Oasis Road have been paying tolls to whoever holds the wells for two thousand years, and they have a very settled opinion of conquerors. {auh_foe} sends a man to your tent with a tray of dried apricots and the rates. There is a rate for an army. It is on the list, between salt and rugs. It is, he says apologetically, per head. He wishes to know if you would like a receipt.

choices.text: Pay the toll, and take the receipt

effects.log: You pay. Your soldiers think it the funniest thing they have ever seen. The wells are open, and you now hold a receipt for an invasion.

choices.text: Offer them the whole road, without tolls, if they open the forts

ok.log: He stops smiling, and goes away to do sums. In a week, two of the forts have somehow been left unlocked.

fail.log: He takes the offer back politely. {auh_foe} has it framed.

events.text: There is a monastery at the head of the pass, with a door that is only tall enough for a child. To go through it, as everyone must, you have to bend. Your scouts tell you it was built that way on purpose, twelve centuries ago, for visiting kings. The abbot has sent word that he would be honoured to give you tea, and that your army is welcome to wait on the other side of the mountain.

choices.text: Bend, and take the tea

effects.log: You bend. The tea has butter in it and is awful. The abbot tells you, as an afterthought, which pass is not defended.

choices.text: Have the door made taller

effects.log: It takes an hour. Your engineers are very neat about it. Every monastery on the plateau knows by nightfall, and they all shut.

events.text: Along the road to {auh_region} every pilgrim you meet is walking the wrong way: towards you, and on their faces, measuring their length on the road, standing, and lying down again. Your scouts have been reporting a large movement of people. It is one old man, you find, and he has been doing this for four years. Your entire column has had to stop, because nobody is willing to march over him.

choices.text: Get down, and walk beside him for a while

effects.log: It is about a mile. By the evening every soldier in the column has heard of it, and the villages have too.

choices.text: Order the column round him and press on

effects.log: They go round, looking at their feet. It costs an hour and something else you could not quite put a name to.

events.text: {auh_foe} comes at you in the old way: a charge straight at your centre, a great shout, and then at thirty paces the whole line of them wheels away, shooting backwards from the saddle. Your front rank has started to run after them. They are good boys. They have never seen this. Behind that long ridge you know, as surely as you know your own name, that there are another ten thousand riders waiting for them.

choices.text: Sound the halt, and hold

ok.log: It is the hardest order you have ever given, and it holds. They wheel twice more, and go home to think about you.

fail.log: The horns are too late for the first three companies. You hold the rest. You can see the ridge, and you know what is behind it.

choices.text: Let them go, and hit the ridge from the side

effects.log: You spend three companies to find the ten thousand. They are gone by morning, and so are your three companies. You took the ridge.

events.text: The Sky Hills are holy. The dead of the Khaganate are laid out on them, and there are large birds there who have been eating well for a thousand years. It is, your engineers say, the only high ground for fifty leagues. The clans are watching to see what you do. {auh_foe} has told them, you hear, exactly what you will do, because it is what everyone does.

choices.text: Camp below the hills, and let your army complain

effects.log: It costs you the high ground and three bad nights. A clan you did not expect sends a rider with salt.

choices.text: Take the high ground. They are only hills

effects.log: It is a very good position. You win from it. No clan will ever speak your name again without spitting.

events.text: A long line of horses has been coming into your lines at dawn, without riders. Your quartermaster is delighted. There are nine hundred of them, fat and sound, and your cavalry has been walking for a month. An old scout is asking to see you. He is not delighted at all. He says the Khaganate does not lose horses, and he would like you to smell their feed.

choices.text: Go and smell it

ok.log: It is sweet, with something in it. By tomorrow every one of those horses would have gone home, at a dead run, with whoever was on them.

fail.log: You smell hay. You are not a horse. It is a very interesting morning, four days later, and a long walk.

choices.text: Keep the horses, but put the scout in charge of them

effects.log: He cuts one open. Then he burns them all, in a straight line, and you can see it from a great way off.

events.text: {auh_foe} has sent you a yurt. It is a very fine one, white felt with a gold roof, and it arrives on forty carts, with a note saying that a person who means to stay should be comfortable. Your officers think it is a joke. Your treasurer thinks it is a bribe. Your physician wants it burned at once. It is getting cold, and you have to admit that it is a very nice yurt.

choices.text: Live in it, in full sight

effects.log: You sleep well. Riders come a long way just to see you sitting in it. There is a kind of courtesy in it the clans can follow.

choices.text: Send it back with a very good horse tied on the front

effects.log: They are delighted, and tell the story against you all winter. Your officers do not get the joke at all.

events.text: Your foragers have found the winter herds of three whole clans in a valley with one way out. It is all the food those clans have, and every soul in them is going to die without it, the very young first. Your own army has been on half rations since the river. {auh_foe} will have to come for them or lose those clans for ever. You hear that the Noyan is, for once, in a great hurry.

choices.text: Take a tenth, and wait for the Noyan by the pass

effects.log: You wait, and the Noyan comes. Those clans watch the fight from the hills, and they do not choose a side, and that is a great deal.

choices.text: Drive them all off and eat

effects.log: Your army eats for the first time in a month. You do not hear what those clans say about it until the spring, and then there are not many left to say it.

events.text: You have been fighting {auh_foe} for a month in a country where the map changes every time it rains. Your scouts have just reported that the Long Ford has moved. Somebody has been cutting dykes upstream at night, very quietly and very well, and your entire left wing is now standing on a pleasant island. It is nearly noon, and the water is still rising, and you can hear singing from the far bank.

choices.text: Boats, rafts, doors: get them off

ok.log: You get them off, on anything that will float. The singing stops about then.

fail.log: You get most of them off. The far bank goes on singing for quite a long time.

choices.text: Tell them to dig in and hold the island

effects.log: They hold it for nine days, and it turns out to be the one place on the delta {auh_foe} did not expect you to be.

events.text: A temple at the river mouth has gone on ringing its bell through three days of your siege. It is very regular. It took your signals officer a long time to notice that it is never quite the same, and that it is telling the barges something. The temple is full of nuns and orphans, and half of them have come to the wall to look at you. Your engineers would like your permission to do something about it.

choices.text: Send up a gift of rice, and a man who reads bells

effects.log: He gets it wrong for a week. Then he gets it right, and for one whole night the barges go exactly where you would like.

choices.text: Give the permission

effects.log: The bell stops. You did not ask how. Up and down the river, every temple starts to ring theirs instead.

events.text: Half your army has the shaking fever, and the other half is carrying them. The herb-wives have told you what it is, and have a very good bark that cures it, and they have told you where it grows, which is in the hills that {auh_foe} holds. A boy has come in under a white cloth, sent over from their lines. He has brought a basket of the bark. There is no note, and he does not know why, and he would like to go home.

choices.text: Use it, and send back a basket of salt

effects.log: Nobody ever says anything about it. Later on, at the end, it is the reason {auh_foe} agrees to see you at all.

choices.text: Have it tested first, on the prisoners

ok.log: It is good bark. Your physicians are sure of that now. The prisoners got better, and they will mention how they found out.

fail.log: It is good bark. You lost a week being careful. The fever did not wait for the result.

events.text: Lakan's old war elephant has come to you. No one led her. She has walked through your pickets in the night, with a broken chain, and now stands at your cook-fire with her trunk in the rice. The mahouts in your prisoner pens have all begun to weep. She is about ninety years old, and she has killed more men than anyone in this war, and according to the entire kingdom she is a bad omen for whoever makes her leave.

choices.text: Let her stay. Feed her

effects.log: She stays. Her name is Mother of Rain, and your soldiers start to bring her fruit. The next village opens its gate before you knock.

choices.text: Give her to the mahouts and send them all home

effects.log: They go, walking beside her, right through the middle of {auh_foe}'s camp, telling everyone who let them.

events.text: Your supply barges are being sunk by something that nobody has seen. Your officers are saying divers. The soldiers say a river serpent, the old one, the one that takes the field with this kingdom's armies. You have been to the bank at night to see for yourself. There is a very long ripple out there, against the current, and an old ferryman who will not look at it. He says the empire has not asked it to stop.

choices.text: Make the offering the ferryman tells you to

ok.log: You feel extremely foolish, up to your knees in the water with a live duck. Nothing sinks for a month.

fail.log: You feel extremely foolish, and you lose the duck, and the barges.

choices.text: Move your supply by land, at twice the cost

effects.log: It is slow and it is dull, and it is out of reach. You never do find out how long it was.

events.text: You have taken the outer wall of {auh_region}. There is a second wall, inside the first, cut into the same rock. The defenders are sitting on it with their swords across their knees. {auh_foe} has had tea sent out to your officers, to be drunk, the messenger says, while they consider the third wall. It seems the architect was a very patient man who disliked visitors. He is buried under the fourth.

choices.text: Find out how the water gets in

ok.log: It gets in by a very small pipe, from a very old cistern. Three days later the tea stops.

fail.log: It gets in from a spring under the fourth wall. The architect thought of that too.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and go on with the ladders

effects.log: It is excellent tea. It costs you a great many ladders, and you do get through the second wall.

events.text: A storm has come up the strait with no warning, the kind the Isles have a name for. Your fleet is tied up in a harbour you took last month, and the sailors you hired here have all gone up the hill without a word, and are sitting on the rocks looking out to sea. {auh_foe} has ships out in it. You can see them, far off, doing something no sane person would do. They are coming in.

choices.text: Cut the anchors and meet them outside the harbour

ok.log: It is the worst day of your life, and it does not stop. In the evening there are no more ships of theirs. There are not very many of yours.

fail.log: You get about a third of the way out of the harbour mouth. The sea and {auh_foe} do the rest between them.

choices.text: Go up the hill and sit with your sailors

effects.log: You watch them come, and you watch the sea break them on your own harbour bar. Your sailors nod to you, and say nothing. You keep the harbour.

events.text: A boy of sixteen has walked into your camp in full armour, by himself, and has asked politely for whoever is in charge. He is {auh_foe}'s second son. He says he has been told that you are the strongest person in the world, and that he would be grateful if you would kill him, as it is the only way that he will ever be mentioned in the family history. He has brought his own mat. You have a war to run.

choices.text: Disarm him in front of the camp, and send him home

effects.log: He does not speak to you. He bows. His father sends a very small sword, and a very long letter.

choices.text: Take him on as your orderly

effects.log: He is an appalling orderly. He takes it extremely seriously. The Isles begin to tell the story, and they get it nearly right.

events.text: The sea lord's envoys are very courteous about your supply fleet. They have, they say, burned none of it. They have merely bought it. Every one of your hired captains now has a house with a garden on the Sword Isles, and the deeds are in their names. They are all still here, at their posts, and every one of them looks exactly as they did before. You are the only person who has been told.

choices.text: Say nothing, and change every sailing order tonight

ok.log: Three of them sail on the wrong tide, straight into your harbour guard. The rest quietly decide that they prefer to be honest.

fail.log: Nothing happens at all, for two whole weeks. It is the sound of a great many people having been warned.

choices.text: Hang the deeds on the mast of the flagship, and buy them back

effects.log: It takes every tael in the chest. They come to you one by one, and they can hardly look at you. They will not take the sea lord's money twice.

events.text: There is an old custom in the Isles. Before the last assault, the two commanders meet, on neutral rock, and compose a poem together, one line each, about the battle that is going to happen. Nobody can tell you why, and {auh_foe} has sent to ask whether you know the form. You do not know the form. Your entire staff are looking at their boots. It has been a long time since anyone asked you for a poem.

choices.text: Go, and do your best

ok.log: You finish on a line about gulls that is not good. {auh_foe} looks at it for a long time, and says it will do. There is less fight in them next morning.

fail.log: Your line does not scan. {auh_foe} is very kind about it. The poem is read out in every harbour in the Isles.

choices.text: Send your best clerk

effects.log: He is very good. They are polite to him. It goes in the records that you sent a clerk, in the place where you would have rather it did not.

events.text: It has snowed in the passes in the wrong month, and you have the Plateau's army trapped at the head of a valley, and it has you trapped at the foot of it. There is one small village between you, and it holds food for one of you, if that. Its headwoman has walked up to your lines through waist-deep drifts to ask you how much of it you were planning to take. {auh_foe} has also had a visit.

choices.text: Offer to share what you have, and split it with the valley

effects.log: It is a thin, cold, very strange winter. In the spring your soldiers and theirs know each other by name, and they are not so eager.

choices.text: Get there first, by night, over the ridge

ok.log: You have the village by dawn. You feed your army. In the spring, {auh_foe}'s is what is left of it.

fail.log: Half of your column goes down the wrong side of the ridge. You find them in the spring.

events.text: The monks of the upper pass do not fight. They have come out and seated themselves across your road, four thousand of them, in rows, in the snow, and begun to chant. It is very beautiful. It has been going on for two days. Your soldiers, who have marched across half the world, have stopped, and they are looking at you. {auh_foe} has very sensibly drawn up behind the monks, with a good view.

choices.text: Go and sit with them, and ask what they want

ok.log: You sit for two days. It turns out that they want the relic road kept open. You can do that. The rows part, slowly, from the middle.

fail.log: You sit for two days. You have a great many thoughts. None of them is any use against a person who is not trying to win.

choices.text: Have the army walk through them, without harming anyone

effects.log: They do it, gently. They carry some of them. It takes all day, and {auh_foe} charges at the end, and your soldiers have no heart in it.

events.text: A caravan has reached you carrying a letter from {auh_foe}. The letter is about money. It seems the Plateau has been lending to your suppliers for a good many years, and to their fathers, at reasonable rates. There is a list of who owes what. It is a long list. There are several names on it you know very well, and one of them is sitting across the fire from you, looking at the fire.

choices.text: Burn the list in front of them all

effects.log: They all watch it go. Nobody says anything. In the morning you have the most loyal quartermasters in the world, and they have no idea how much you read.

choices.text: Quietly buy up the debts yourself

ok.log: It costs a great deal and it takes a season, and then the whole of the Oasis Road owes you and not them.

fail.log: The Plateau has a much longer memory for figures than you do. You have bought several debts twice.

events.text: Your cannon, the ones it took eleven hundred men to drag up here, have just been fired at the wall of Norbu's fort, for the first time. It turns out that black powder is a different thing at this height. You are told you were lucky that you were standing at the back. The fort's garrison have come up on the wall to see, and someone there has started a slow, polite round of applause.

choices.text: Ask the prisoners who built the fort

ok.log: He is eighty and he is in your pens. He is very rude about the fort. He knows where the mortar was stinted, and he has been waiting a long time to tell someone.

fail.log: He is eighty, and he is in your pens, and he says it cannot be done. He seems quite sure.

choices.text: Bow to the wall, and start digging

effects.log: They applaud that too. The digging takes four months, and at the end of it they stop applauding.

events.text: A great white lion has been seen on the ridge above your camp, three evenings running, and the whole army has seen it. It does nothing. Your soldiers have started to leave food out. You are told this is the very beast that has walked with the Plateau's armies since the first of its kings, and that when it walks down to your side of the valley the empire has been lost. Tonight it has come a little way down.

choices.text: Walk up alone and look back at it

effects.log: You stand there about an hour, and it is a very cold hour. It goes back over the ridge. Nobody on either side of the valley knows what that means, and they are all telling each other.

choices.text: Set a double guard, and go to bed

effects.log: Nothing comes in the night. It is a sensible order. Some of the men are a little sorry, and so, you notice, are you.

events.text: {auh_region} is yours. The clans stand in their ranks on the trampled grass. {auh_foe} has been brought to you with a rope around one wrist, quite unashamed, and is examining your horses. Up here, you have been told, what a conqueror does next is the only thing that will ever be remembered. They already have a word for what you are, and three words for what you might be.

choices.text: Cut the rope. Offer {auh_foe} a command

effects.log: They look at you for a while. "Who feeds my horses?" they ask. It is not a yes. By evening it is.

choices.text: Keep the clans' own chiefs, under your tribute

effects.log: They accept without a flicker. Everyone here has paid tribute to someone. It is not the same as being beaten.

choices.text: Build forts on every well

effects.log: It takes a lot of timber, in a place with none. Nobody can water a horse now without being counted.

choices.text: Let the army have the herds

effects.log: The army eats. The clans watch it, with no expression at all, and they begin to teach it to their children.

events.text: The Salt Pasture has come to you with its herds and without its young men. The old women do the talking here. One of them wants to know, without any fuss, whether you are the kind that stays or the kind that goes home, because they will need to know how to count the lambs. She has seen both. It has taken your whole staff a week to work out that she is not joking about the lambs.

choices.text: "I stay. Count them for me, and keep nine in ten."

effects.log: She counts them as if you had said nothing remarkable. But the lambs come, and so, in a year or two, do the young men.

choices.text: Leave a garrison and a tax clerk

effects.log: The clerk writes that the lambs are very few this year. They will go on being very few as long as he lives.

choices.text: Take the whole of the year's lambs for the army

effects.log: She nods, as if a thing were confirmed. There is nobody to count anything next year.

events.text: You have taken {auh_region}, and it took the Khaganate about a week to stop looking for it. Its clans have just moved, without any fuss, about two hundred miles north, leaving you a very large quantity of grass. A few of them have stayed. They are the ones nobody else wanted, the lame and the feuding and a shaman with a grudge. They would very much like to know what you are offering.

choices.text: Offer them the whole of it

effects.log: They look at each other. It is the first time anyone has ever offered them anything. You now have the most loyal province on the steppe.

choices.text: Put your own people on the grass

effects.log: Your settlers arrive in good heart, with ploughs. The grass is very patient, and so is everyone else.

choices.text: Ride after the ones who left

effects.log: You catch up with some of them. It is not a thing the songs will thank you for.

events.text: {auh_foe} has been brought in, by boat, under an awning, with a very good breakfast. You have the Terrace Country from the river to the cloud line, and every one of those terraces was built by hand, and takes all year to keep. In this country, the abbots remind you, nobody has ever conquered anything. People just arrive, and after a while they are paying the same taxes in a different language.

choices.text: Leave the temples and the water law as they are

effects.log: The water runs. The abbots bow. In ten years your own soldiers are growing rice and will not hear a word against it.

choices.text: Give {auh_foe} a command of their own

effects.log: They finish the breakfast first. "In which direction?" they ask. It is not a thing anyone could call loyalty, but it is a great deal of use.

choices.text: Set your own magistrates over the water

effects.log: They are honest men, and they know nothing about water. It is a hard few years on the terraces.

choices.text: Strip the temple roofs

effects.log: It is an astonishing amount of gold. The terraces begin to fail in the third year, one above another, slowly.

events.text: There is nobody in {auh_region} who has not lost someone to your barges. Now the Temple Delta is yours, and they have all come down to the water with lamps, thousands and thousands of them, and they are setting them on the river for the dead. It is the same every year, they say. It would be going on with or without you. Your army stands on the bank, a little way back. Nobody has told them what to do.

choices.text: Set one down yourself, for both sides

effects.log: It floats away with the rest. No one looks at you. An old woman moves over slightly, to make room.

choices.text: Post guards, and let it be

effects.log: It goes on until dawn. Nothing happens. They were counting your guards, but then they count everything.

choices.text: Clear the bank. It is an unlawful assembly

effects.log: It takes all night. For the next forty years, nobody on the Delta will tell you the time of day.

events.text: The Elephant Fords are yours, and you have also acquired four hundred elephants, who eat more than your whole army and all know exactly who is in charge. It is not you. There are also their mahouts, who will starve without them, and {auh_foe}, who has trained every one of them from the calf and is sitting under guard, staring at the wall. An elephant in the yard has begun to call, and will not stop.

choices.text: Give {auh_foe} back the elephant corps, under your banner

effects.log: The calling stops. You have made a very dangerous friend. Your own cavalry is beside itself.

choices.text: Keep the corps as your own, under your officers

effects.log: It costs a good deal, and two of your officers. In the end they have an understanding, of a kind.

choices.text: Sell them to the Temple Delta

effects.log: The price is excellent. Nobody on either side of the river thinks well of it.

events.text: {auh_foe} has come down the rock to you with the keys on a tray, and the sword held flat in both hands, and has knelt. It is done very beautifully. By the custom of the Isles you may now say one of three things: "Keep it", or "Give it to me", or nothing. You have been warned about nothing. A retainer stands behind them with a short blade and a clean white cloth, and is plainly hoping you will be sensible.

choices.text: "Keep it. You serve me now."

effects.log: They stand. They will be yours from now on with an untroubled mind, and it is rather frightening how much they mean it.

choices.text: "Give it to me", and put your own lord in the castle

effects.log: You take it. The retainer bows, and takes the cloth away. Your lord in the castle will have a very interesting time.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. It is over in a moment. Nobody on the Isles will ever call it cruel, and nobody will ever trust you with their children.

events.text: The Outer Harbours are full of ships and of people who would very much like to know whether they are still allowed to trade. The harbour guild has sent up a very small man with a very large book. It has the customs of every port from here to the Morning Isles, and he would like you to know that he has been the customs officer for three sea lords in succession. He does not seem to think you are likely to be the last.

choices.text: Keep him on, at his old rates

effects.log: The ships go on sailing. You are the first conqueror he has ever bothered to look up at, and only for a moment.

choices.text: Lower the harbour dues and let them all know why

effects.log: The harbours fill. They do not love you, but they are getting rich, and they will fight anyone who says it should stop.

choices.text: Seize the ships, and the book

effects.log: You have a lot of ships now. Nobody who knows how to sail them will talk to you.

events.text: The Reef Castles have surrendered, and so has the whole Sword School attached to them, three hundred students, kneeling on the rock in the rain with their swords laid in front of them. {auh_foe} has told you, quite calmly, that the young ones do not yet know how to do anything except fight duels for rank, and that this will be your problem now.

choices.text: Keep the school open, and send them against the next castle

effects.log: They are very happy, and they are a terror. It is the first time they have been asked to do something they understand.

choices.text: Scatter them through your own army

effects.log: Your sergeants have a great deal to say about it. By the next campaign you have some strange and excellent squads.

choices.text: Close the school and melt the blades

effects.log: It makes a very large bell. You can hear it across the strait. So can everybody else.

events.text: The caravan masters of the Oasis Road have come in a body to congratulate you. They are extremely pleased that you have taken {auh_region}. They were extremely pleased about the last one, too. They have brought the books, and they would like to know how you feel about tolls in general. Behind them in a very respectful row, {auh_foe} stands under guard, and is the only one in the tent who looks at you straight.

choices.text: Leave the tolls, and ask {auh_foe} to keep the road for you

effects.log: The masters go a very odd colour. {auh_foe} takes a long breath. You are going to hear a great deal about those books.

choices.text: Cut the tolls by half, and put your own clerks on them

effects.log: The road gets busy, and your clerks get rich. There is not a lot you can do about both of those things at once.

choices.text: Hang the masters, and take the books

effects.log: The road goes quiet from one end to the other. You have the books. You cannot read them, as it turns out. Nobody can, except them.

events.text: The Monastery Passes are yours. {auh_foe} has come down to you on foot, with nothing, and asked only that you leave the scripture houses alone. It would take you a hundred years to read them. Your treasurer has also been up there, and tells you that the scripture is written in gold, on silver, and it is really a very great deal of gold. The whole plateau is holding quite still and waiting to hear.

choices.text: Leave them, and post a guard against your own army

effects.log: It costs you a very good sum in what the army thinks it is owed. Pilgrims come up the road again in the spring.

choices.text: Tax the monasteries, at the rate they tax their villages

effects.log: They are shocked. Then they send you the accounts. It is a surprisingly small sum, and you begin to understand a good deal about the plateau.

choices.text: Melt it

effects.log: It takes forty furnaces. You can pay your army for ten years. There is no one on the plateau now who will carry anything for you.

events.text: The garrison of the Caravan Forts marched out with its drums going and its flags up, because Norbu has insisted on it, and you agreed. There are a great many women and children walking behind them. It turns out that a fort out here is really a town. They are heading off into a great deal of empty country, and winter is about six weeks away. {auh_foe} has not asked you for anything at all.

choices.text: Call them back, with all their people, and give them the forts

effects.log: Nobody cheers. But they turn around, and they are still there the next year, and they keep your road for you.

choices.text: Send wagons of grain after them

effects.log: It is not much. They take it without a word. Some of them reach somewhere.

choices.text: Let them go. You keep your word and no more

effects.log: You hold the forts. It is a very long way to see, on a clear day, from the wall.

events.text: You have found the Moving City, and it has stopped moving. {auh_ruler} comes out of the great white tent in full armour, a good deal older than any of the songs, and rides the last hundred paces alone. In all the long history of the steppe, no Khagan has ever been taken alive. They stop a little way off, and look over your whole host, with interest, and then they ask you how you have kept your horses alive.

choices.text: Tell them, and offer them the steppe as your governor

effects.log: It is the longest talk of your life. They take the post without kneeling. It is as near to it as anyone will get.

choices.text: Give them a good horse and an open road north

effects.log: They look at the horse first. They ride off without thanking you. There will be a story about that horse.

choices.text: Finish it, as a Khagan ought to be finished

effects.log: They would not have had it otherwise, and they say so. The whole host stands silent, on both sides, until it is over.

events.text: {auh_ruler} is not here. The Moving City has been left for you, every tent in its place, every fire banked, a pot still warm. There is a child sitting on the high seat, swinging their feet. It seems that this is the Khagan's youngest grandchild. By steppe law whoever holds the seat holds the empire, and they have been told to stay here and to tell you that you may have it, if you can get them to move.

choices.text: Sit down on the ground in front of them, and talk

effects.log: It takes the whole afternoon. They would like a horse, it turns out. The clans come in by the thousand to see how it ends.

choices.text: Lift the child off, gently, and take the seat

effects.log: They bite you. It is what you would have done. Then they are put on a very good horse, and sent where the Khagan went.

choices.text: Hold them hostage against the Khagan's return

effects.log: It works. {auh_ruler} comes back, alone, for the child. The whole steppe will know how you got them to come.

events.text: The Golden Barge City has opened all nine of its water gates to you, and it has done so with music. {auh_ruler} waits under a canopy at the landing stage, surrounded by a very great number of priests, and offers you a garland and a cup. Your food taster has gone quiet. Every report you have had of this court says that nobody has ever defeated it. They have just been outlived, and invited to dinner.

choices.text: Raise the cup, and pour it on the water

effects.log: It smells of only wine. {auh_ruler} smiles for the first time. "Most do not," they say, and they will run the delta for you with enormous skill.

choices.text: Have them step down, and go to the Temple of the Last River

effects.log: They go, on foot, with their whole court walking behind them. It takes a day. Half of the city goes too, and it may not be a mercy.

choices.text: Have the whole court taken in chains

effects.log: They go without any fuss. All Nine Rivers start to sing a song about you. It goes very slowly and it never stops.

events.text: The elephants have knelt. All along the Avenue of Rain they have gone down on their knees, as they do for a coronation, because some old mahout has told them to, and {auh_ruler} is walking out between them without any guards, and carrying a small plain box. The people of the city are all on the roofs, and no one is making a sound. In the box, they tell you, is the earth of all Nine Rivers. You may take it, or not.

choices.text: Open it, take a pinch, and hand the box back

effects.log: A sound goes across the rooftops, not a cheer. You rule them now, and they rule it for you. You will find out which of those is true.

choices.text: Take the box

effects.log: It is lighter than you expected. {auh_ruler} goes into exile with empty hands. The rains are late that year.

choices.text: Empty it into the river, in front of them all

effects.log: It takes a moment. You are told that the sound the city makes will be remembered, and it is.

events.text: The Morning Gate has fallen. You have climbed to the top of the highest keep, with very little breath left, and {auh_ruler} is waiting there alone on a mat, in white, with the sea behind them, and a blade laid out on a cloth. They are perfectly composed. They would like you to witness it, and to say a few words about it afterwards. It is the highest thing that one person can ask of another. It is a very fine morning.

choices.text: Sit down in front of them, and ask them to rule for you instead

effects.log: They look at you for the first time with real surprise. It is a long time before they answer. The blade goes back in its cloth.

choices.text: Put the blade in the sea and put them on a ship

effects.log: They are not grateful. It is much the worst thing that you could have done to them. They live for thirty years.

choices.text: Witness it, and say the words

effects.log: You do it properly. Every one of the Isles will speak of how well you did it, and it will not help you sleep.

events.text: There are three hundred ships in the roads at Morning Gate, flying the white flag of the sea lords, and {auh_ruler} has come aboard your flagship, alone, by a rope ladder. The sea does not belong to anyone, they point out. You may have every rock, castle and harbour in the Isles, with their blessing. They and the ships will simply go on being out there, and you can work out for yourself what that means.

choices.text: Appoint them Admiral of All Your Seas

effects.log: They think about it for the time it takes to fill a pipe. It may be that no one has ever got the better of you so completely.

choices.text: Let them sail: and keep the harbours

effects.log: They go over the horizon, with all their ships, on the morning tide. You will have to be very careful about the sea for a while.

choices.text: Keep them aboard, and burn the ships

effects.log: It takes all night, and you can see it from four islands. You own the Isles, and no one else will sail for you.

events.text: You have reached the White Palace by its thousand steps, on foot, because there is no other way. {auh_ruler} is at the top, where they have been sitting for some time, with a pot of tea and an expression of mild interest. It seems that they have always known about you. There is a very old prophecy about this, and it has been read to you already. You have not yet been told what it says about you afterwards.

choices.text: Ask them to read you the rest, and to stay on and teach you

effects.log: They laugh until they have to put down the tea. They stay. You rule the plateau, and you are, in some way you cannot quite pin down, its student.

choices.text: Send them to a far monastery with their books

effects.log: They go at a walking pace, and they leave the pot. The plateau watches them leave for a very long time.

choices.text: Burn the prophecy, and the court with it

effects.log: The fire can be seen a long way off. Paper burns very well up here. The monks have all of it by heart.

events.text: {auh_ruler} is a child of six, chosen at the age of two by a lot of monks, who found them in a village by the way they looked at a bell. The whole court has fled in the night. The child is here on the great throne, with one very old servant. They are asking for you to come closer, because they cannot see you very well from up there. Somebody has dressed them properly. Their feet do not reach the floor.

choices.text: Kneel where they can see you, and make them your ward

effects.log: They give it some thought, and then they ask if you have ever seen an elephant. It seems you are the regent of the plateau now.

choices.text: Send them home to their village, with the old servant

effects.log: They were only ever a child from a village. In three years the plateau has found another, and in ten it will find you.

choices.text: Take the throne, and leave no doubt

effects.log: It is quick, and quiet, and you did not do it yourself. Nobody on the plateau will ever say a word about it where you can hear.

events.text: It is over. {auh_foe} has held {auh_region} against you, and {auh_host} is going back along the road that it came by, in fairly good order, carrying what it can. You count what is left, and then you make yourself count it again. A very young officer asks where you would like the rearguard. It is a good question. It is much the most useful thing that anyone has said to you this month.

choices.text: Take the rearguard yourself

effects.log: You come off the field last. Nobody will thank you for it. They do remember, and next spring they turn out again.

choices.text: Ride ahead, and start planning the next one

effects.log: You are home before the news is. There are some who will say that is not the same as winning.

events.text: The dispatch from {auh_region} has reached your tent, and the person who brought it would rather be anywhere else. You have lost the campaign, and you lost it for a reason so stupid that nobody has dared to put it in writing. It was the boots. Somebody bought forty thousand pairs of boots from a cousin. You are going to have to find out whose. {auh_foe} has sent a pair back to you, with a note.

choices.text: Find the cousin

effects.log: It takes a month. You make very sure that every quartermaster in the host hears what happened to the cousin.

choices.text: Wear the boots home

effects.log: They are as bad as you thought. Every soldier on that road sees you limping, and for a little while they stop cursing you.

events.text: You thought that you had {auh_region}. For one whole afternoon you had it. Then {auh_foe} did something on the left that your best officers are still drawing in the dirt, trying to understand. You have ordered the retreat. You can hear them singing across the valley. You realise, with an odd detachment, that you would very much like to meet this person, and that you are not going to be asked.

choices.text: Send a good horse across, with your compliments

effects.log: It comes back in a week, better groomed. So now you know each other. It is going to make the next time a good deal worse.

choices.text: Learn the left by heart

effects.log: You have it drawn on your wall by the winter. You look at it instead of eating. You do not get it wrong twice.

events.text: There is nothing to be said about {auh_region}. {auh_Host} has gone in, and has not come out, not all of it, and there are a great many letters that will have to be written. The clerks offer you the usual form of words. There is a space in it for the name. You look at the list of names for some time. You had not known that the list would be so long, and you find you know quite a few of them.

choices.text: Write them yourself

effects.log: It takes the whole winter. Your hand is never quite the same. Some of the replies are not what you would like to read.

choices.text: Sign the clerks' forms

effects.log: It takes an afternoon. You have a war to run. You do not look at the list again, and you do know where it is.

events.text: You have been beaten in {auh_region} by {auh_foe}, in front of everybody. That part you can stand. What you cannot quite stand is that in every town along the road home they have already put your name up on the wall, in chalk, with a little drawing. The children have made up a skipping song. It is rather catchy. You catch yourself humming it at a staff meeting, and your staff all look very hard at the table.

choices.text: Have them taught the second verse

effects.log: You write it yourself. It is ruder than theirs, and it is about you. It is sung in the ranks for years.

choices.text: Have the chalk washed off

effects.log: It is back by morning, in every town along the road. It is rather better drawn.

events.text: {auh_foe} has you where they want you, in {auh_region}, in a valley with one way out, and has sent a messenger up to say that you may leave it. All of you. You need only sign a paper saying that you came here by mistake. It is written out neatly. Your officers are pretending that they cannot read. It is very hot. There is some dust coming up the valley, and you can tell by now what kind of dust it is.

choices.text: Sign it, and bring them all home

effects.log: You sign. You bring them home. It will be read out in the courts of three empires, and every one of the people you brought home knows what you did.

choices.text: Tear it up and go through them

effects.log: You go through them. It takes a day. You do come out the other side, with those who are left.

events.text: A rider has come from the other front: {auh_gen} has taken {auh_region}. The dispatch is two lines long. {ag_He} does not ask for anything. {ag_He} mentions the weather, and the state of the mules. Your staff have been hanging on your face while you read it. You have a war of your own to finish, and you find that you are grinning at a sheet of paper, like a fool, over two lines about mules.

choices.text: Send {ag_him} your own horse

effects.log: It is a very good horse. {ag_He} will not ride it, you hear. {ag_He} has it led behind the column, for the soldiers to look at.

choices.text: Send more mules

effects.log: {ag_He} writes back one word. Your staff think it is a joke, and you are fairly sure.

events.text: {auh_gen} has taken {auh_region}, and you have the whole story of it from three different people, none of whom was in the room. It seems that {ag_he} did it with about a tenth of the army that you would have used. It seems that you would not have thought of it. {ag_His} own soldiers have started to cut {ag_his} name on their spear shafts. You have just been told this as if it were good news.

choices.text: Say in public that it is the best thing done in this war

effects.log: You say it where it will get back. It costs you something, and it gets back. The soldiers on the other front stop looking over their shoulders.

choices.text: Thank {ag_him}, in the usual form

effects.log: The usual form is quite correct. Your clerks know it is the usual form, and so does {auh_gen}.

events.text: The people of {auh_region} have come out to meet {auh_gen} on the road, with rice and paper flowers. {ag_He} had told the army that anyone who took so much as a chicken would answer for it, and then {ag_he} made them all watch while {ag_he} paid for a chicken. It is the talk of the empire. Your tax clerks have arrived behind {ag_him} and are not very pleased to see how little there is left to shout at.

choices.text: Put {ag_him} in charge of the clerks as well

effects.log: It is a great deal of power to hand to one person. The tax comes in, and it comes in early, and without a single chicken.

choices.text: Back the clerks. A province must learn to pay

effects.log: They learn to pay. {auh_gen} says nothing about it in {ag_his} next three letters. They are very short letters.

events.text: {auh_gen} has taken {auh_region}, and has also taken the wrong people along with it: four hundred nobles who fought for the other side, who have all surrendered to {ag_him} personally, because they were told {ag_he} was fair. {ag_He} would like to know what you intend to do with them. {ag_He} says it very politely. It is the first time in all these years that you have seen {ag_him} put a question in writing.

choices.text: Say that {ag_his} word is your word

effects.log: They go home. Every noble in the next province starts to think about it. So does {auh_gen}, and {ag_he} never mentions it again.

choices.text: Have them sent to you in chains

effects.log: They come. {ag_He} sends them on the day your order arrives, with a clerk. {ag_He} has not told you what {ag_he} told them.

events.text: You have a very odd letter from {auh_gen}. {ag_He} has taken {auh_region}, it says at the bottom, in passing, but the point of the letter is a recipe for a cold noodle dish that {ag_he} has had up there. {ag_He} thinks that you would like it. {ag_He} has drawn a picture of the noodles. Your staff are astonished that you have stopped the war to read it out to them, and you send for the cook.

choices.text: Have it made for the whole staff

effects.log: It is really very good. It becomes a thing you do, on your front, after every victory. You write and tell {ag_him}.

choices.text: Send back a recipe of your own

effects.log: Yours is not as good. {ag_He} is too polite to say so, and {ag_he} says so.

events.text: {auh_gen} has lost the front at {auh_region}. The dispatch is in {ag_his} own hand, and it does not offer a reason. It gives the numbers. {ag_He} has brought back what could be brought back, and {ag_he} is waiting at the crossing, under no one's guard, for you to send whatever it is you are going to send. The army over there is watching that crossing, and so is your army, and so is everyone else.

choices.text: Send a new horse, and a new army

effects.log: It is a large thing to give to someone who has just lost. {ag_He} does not write back. {ag_He} gets on the horse.

choices.text: Send an inquiry

effects.log: It finds that nobody could have done better, as it happens. It takes eight months to find it, and everyone knows who ordered it.

events.text: They are saying on your front that {auh_gen} lost because you did not send the grain. You did send the grain. It went by way of an officer of yours, and it stayed with him, and you have only found this out now that the front is gone. {ag_He} has not said one word about it, and {ag_he} has all the letters. You have just been handed a list of the dead from {auh_region}, and there is a great deal of it.

choices.text: Hang the officer, and say why

effects.log: You say why, out loud, on parade. It costs you some face, and it buys you more than you could have paid for.

choices.text: Quietly replace him

effects.log: You replace him. It is the sensible way. {ag_He} hears about it, the way that {ag_he} hears about everything.

events.text: {auh_gen} has come home from {auh_region} on a door. Six of {ag_his} soldiers have been carrying {ag_him}, in turn, for a hundred miles, and they will not set {ag_him} down for your physicians until you have told them to in person. {ag_He} is awake. {ag_He} tells you, very clearly, exactly what {ag_he} did wrong, in order, with the times. You had better write it down. There is nobody else alive who knows.

choices.text: Write it down yourself, every word

effects.log: It takes all night. It turns out to be the best thing anyone has written about that country. {ag_He} sleeps after that.

choices.text: Tell {ag_him} to rest, and send for a clerk

effects.log: The clerk gets most of it. {ag_He} watches you leave, and {ag_he} does not say anything else about it.

events.text: You have the news from {auh_region}. {auh_gen} fell back, and fell back again, and in the end {ag_he} had to give up a city with its people still in it. There is a delegation here from that city, the ones who got out. They have asked to see {auh_gen} and then they have asked to see you, and they would like to know what it was that your war was for, exactly. They have come a long way and they will wait.

choices.text: See them yourself, and hear all of it

effects.log: It takes two days. You give them no answer they can use. They are the only people in the empire who ever got one from you at all.

choices.text: Have them given money and sent home

effects.log: It is quite a lot of money. They take it, and go. They left a list behind them, on your steward's table.

events.text: {auh_gen} has written from the other front. It is not a report. It says that it is raining there, and that {ag_he} has been thinking about the first time you met, and what you said about {ag_his} boots. {ag_He} has been a long way from home for a long time. At the bottom, in smaller writing, {ag_he} asks whether you ever think about stopping. You read it twice. You have three hundred things to sign.

choices.text: Write back that night, by your own hand

effects.log: It takes two hours, with all you have to do. You do not really answer the question. You do mention the boots.

choices.text: Have a clerk send the usual reply

effects.log: He does it very nicely. You do not get another of those letters.

events.text: There has been a marriage, on the other front. {auh_gen} writes to tell you, somewhat stiffly, that one of {ag_his} captains has married a woman of the country, and then four hundred of the soldiers have done the same. {ag_He} feels that you ought to know. {ag_He} has been asked by the priests of both sides if this means that they are now one people, and {ag_he} would like to know what {ag_he} ought to tell them.

choices.text: Tell them yes

effects.log: You send silver for the weddings. It costs less than one battle would. There are some children there now who are going to be very difficult to conquer.

choices.text: Forbid it. An army is not a colony

effects.log: The order is read out. It is obeyed, as far as anyone can see. The priests have a good long laugh about it, on both sides.

events.text: {auh_gen} wants you to know about a soldier called Pak, who held a bridge. The rest of the letter is about Pak: where he was from, that he owed his sister money, that he could not sing. {ag_He} has been writing letters like this one for some years now, you realise, and you have them all in a box. It has occurred to you that {ag_he} has never once written you a letter about {ag_him}.

choices.text: Pay what Pak owed his sister

effects.log: You have it done from your own purse, with a note. It goes all round the front, somehow. It was about four taels.

choices.text: Add it to the box

effects.log: You put it with the others. You mean to do something about that box, one of these days, when all of this is over.

events.text: A letter from {auh_gen}, and a package. {ag_He} sends you, with {ag_his} compliments, a pair of very warm boots, made by an old woman on the other front who had heard that it is cold where you are. There is a note from the old woman too, or rather a mark. She is, {ag_he} explains, the mother of someone your army killed. {ag_He} does not explain any more. You have put them on. They really are very warm boots.

choices.text: Send her something, without a name on it

effects.log: She sends it back. She knows perfectly well who it is from. You go on wearing the boots.

choices.text: Ask {ag_him} what she wanted

effects.log: Nothing, {ag_he} writes. {ag_He} asked her that too. She said you looked cold.

events.text: A man has come to you from the other front at great personal risk, a colonel of {auh_gen}'s, with something he thinks that you should know. The soldiers have started to call {auh_gen} by a title that nobody has given {ag_him}. Last week they brought out a yellow cloak at dinner. {ag_He} sent it back, he says. But {ag_he} did look at it, for just a moment. He wants that to be understood.

choices.text: Do nothing. Send {ag_him} the colonel's letter, unopened

effects.log: You send it across. {ag_He} reads it, and burns it, and the colonel is moved to the stores. You will not get another chance to find out.

choices.text: Recall {ag_him} for "consultations"

effects.log: The order goes out. It is the most dangerous letter that you have ever signed. It takes three weeks to know how it came out.

choices.text: Take the army off {ag_him}, now, and put it under three people

effects.log: The three people hate each other, which is the point. {auh_gen} comes home in a plain cart. {ag_He} does not write any more about noodles.

events.text: {auh_gen} now governs an area of the world that would take a good rider two months to cross. {ag_He} collects its taxes, and {ag_he} appoints its judges. You have just read through the accounts for that whole front, and every last copper is exactly where it should be. Your Grand Secretary has just asked you, very quietly, if that is not the most alarming thing about it.

choices.text: Tell him that it is the best news of the war

effects.log: He bows, and goes out. You read the books through again, at night, and they are still correct.

choices.text: Bring {ag_him} home with every honour, and keep {ag_him} here

effects.log: {ag_He} comes at once, with one servant. {ag_He} is very bad at the capital. {ag_His} front begins, slowly, to go wrong.

choices.text: Send your own people to divide up the post

effects.log: They go in with your seal and they find everything in order, and a very polite, very cold welcome.

events.text: Somebody in your own household has been writing to {auh_gen}, you find. It is a person very close to {auh_kin}. It seems to be a fairly simple question, put in the politest terms: what, exactly, would {ag_he} do, if you were to die this year? You have the reply here in your hand, unopened. It came to you by way of the courier service that {ag_he} set up. {ag_He} must have known that you would read it.

choices.text: Burn it without reading it, in front of the household

effects.log: The whole house sees you do it. You do have a fair idea what it said, and now so do they. They all sleep a little worse.

choices.text: Read it

effects.log: It says "Mourn." That is all. It is the only word on the page, and you sit there holding it for a long time.

choices.text: Have {ag_him} watched, from now on

effects.log: You find some very good people to do it. {ag_He} gives them dinner. {ag_He} is really very good about it.

events.text: The empires have always had a very simple way of dealing with a general like {auh_gen}, and you have it now in the form of a request from your own ministers. A great feast, and then {ag_he} will be given a title and a garden, and the army will be given to a person who has not won anything. That is how it has been done for two thousand years. They have all the histories here to show you. They have marked the pages.

choices.text: Close the books. {ag_He} keeps the army

effects.log: They look at you the way people look at someone walking on a frozen river in spring. You keep your general. You keep walking.

choices.text: Give the feast

effects.log: It is a very good feast. {ag_He} understands what it is by the second course. {ag_He} raises a cup to you across the room.

events.text: It is done. A letter has come in, and it is in {auh_gen}'s own hand, and very short. {ag_He} is sorry. It has been coming for a long time, and it was not about you, and the soldiers would have done it anyway with or without {ag_him}. {ag_He} is taking {auh_region} with {ag_him}, and {ag_he} asks you, as a favour, not to send anyone {ag_he} knows. You have every letter {ag_he} has ever written in a box beside you.

choices.text: Send someone {ag_he} knows

effects.log: You send the one person who could do it. It is what you would have told anyone else to do. You keep the box.

choices.text: Write back: "I know."

effects.log: You have no idea if {ag_he} gets it. There is a war on, and now it is a larger war.

events.text: They have crowned {auh_gen} in {auh_region}. You hear it from a cook. {ag_He} did not want it, by all accounts, and they brought the yellow cloak out once too often and {ag_he} got tired of saying no. The ones who are telling you all this are very frightened. You had been warned about this. You had had it written down for you with the dates. You find you are mostly thinking about those notes on the boots.

choices.text: Have the war room moved. It is only one more front

effects.log: You have the map redrawn before dinner. Your staff are terrified of how calm you are. So, after a while, are you.

choices.text: Send {ag_him} a congratulation, and your terms

effects.log: The terms are generous. {ag_He} keeps the letter. It is said that {ag_he} keeps it on {ag_his} desk.

events.text: {auh_gen} has gone over.
